title: Taswell Baird arrested at the Juarez border with the bag
summary: Waiting in El Paso, Malachi lingers in shops while his roommate crosses to Juarez and is caught by the Border Patrol, vanishing for months.

story.theme_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and rough clubs of Prohibition
story.community_name: Gangsters, bootleggers and the Prohibition-era clubs

blocks.x: At that particular time, I think I was rooming with Taswell Baird, little Joe we called him, the trombone player. And so he and I, when all this stuff was happening in Texas and these guys were buying all this stuff, he tells me... He said, "Don't bother. We'll get us a small bag, and when we get to El Paso, I know a Mexican over in Juarez and he'll give me (I forgot how much he said) for little or nothing." So he and I were roommates, we're brothers, so I say, "Okay, whatever you say." It was my first time out there. And he had been with Jay McShann's band, and he knew all the West
very well. So he said, "Now, when we get into El Paso, we'll just stash our bags and we'll walk over. It's only a few blocks, and we'll walk over to Juarez."

So we did just that, and put our bags away, and were on our way walking toward Juarez. I was always fascinated by guns and things, and of course, down there in the pawn shops and the stores, they had a whole lot of gear from the Old West, like boots and spears and ten-gallon hats and all kinds of old guns and things in the windows. So I'm walking along, but I'm gawking in these windows at these things, you know. So he's saying, "Come on, man, come on." He's rushing me. So I'l telling him, I'm saying, "Okay, okay, I'm coming." And we walk a few more stores, and I see something else that was interesting. Finally, one store I saw, I wanted to go in.

So he's getting very perturbed with me. In fact, we went in the store and I was looking at something. So he kind of blew up, and he said, "Man, I'm gone." I said, "Well, man, if you want to go, go ahead." He kind of had me pissed, too. I said, "If you want, go ahead!" So he left me. Then I was free to shop or walk around or do whatever I felt like doing.

Anyway, I went on and he went on over to Juarez. So when we got close to the train time, everybody's beginning to gather back at the station. Everybody says, "Hey, man, what did you do?" "I did this" and "I did that," and we're

talking. And we looking around, checking, and it's getting close to time. "Where's so-and-so? Where' Art?" "Art? He's downstairs in the men's room. He'll be back." "Where's so-and-so-and-so." Then it's close to time: "Has anybody seen Little Joe?" Nobody's seen Little Joe anywhere. So finally, train time is here, but no Little Joe. Finally, the train leaves. No Little Joe.

What happened was, this little bag that we had bought, Joe was the one that carried it all the time. And when we went over to Juarez, he took it and he stashed it behind a tree or something before he went across the border. He went over there, he never found the Mexican guy he was looking for, and he came back and went behind the tree to pick up his bag, and he was looking for it, and the Border Patrol came up and handed it to him! That was in January, and I didn't see him no more until September of the next year. It was a tragic thing, you know, but... It was a good six months before I saw him again. It was just one of those incidents, but as I said, it was during the War, and all...
